status: Updated October 7, 2026: adds article cards and the semicircle hype gauge. Updated October 6, 2026: headlines are the loud claims people actually hear, each with a real public source and its own score; the careful versions stay on the dial.

water.headline: Every AI-written email uses a bottle of water.

keyWord.explanation: The estimate was for one 100-word email from one AI model, GPT-4, using guesses about cooling and power. Nobody measured every AI email.

water.scoreReason: The headline treats a computer estimate as if someone measured it, and turns one AI model's email into every AI email.

claimDial.text: AI data centers threaten water supplies in some dry US towns.
claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: AI data centers are guzzling water in some dry US towns.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

W1.reason: “Guzzling” adds drama the evidence doesn't need.

claimDial.text: AI data centers are guzzling the water in America's dry towns.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P2.reason: Talks about all dry towns, when the evidence covers some places.

W1.reason: “Guzzling” adds drama the evidence doesn't need.

claimDial.text: Every AI-written email uses a bottle of water.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: AI is greedily drinking America dry and will leave us all without water.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States as fact something no evidence shows.

P2.reason: Stretches local strain to the whole country.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W1.reason: “Drinking America dry” is alarm, not evidence.

W2.reason: Treats AI as greedy, when companies decide where to build.

finePrint.label: Not all data centers are AI
finePrint.text: Most water figures cover every kind of data center, from email to video streaming, so not all of it is AI.

finePrint.label: Some water goes back
finePrint.text: Data centers take water from rivers and wells. Some of it is returned. The part that evaporates is what a town really loses.

finePrint.label: Hot days matter most
finePrint.text: A data center can look small over a year but use a lot on the hottest days, when water is scarcest.

finePrint.label: Saving water costs power
finePrint.text: Cooling systems that use less water need more electricity, so there's no free fix.

finePrint.label: Where the bottle number comes from
finePrint.text: Researchers estimated it for one 100-word email from GPT-4, counting water at the data center and at the power plant. It's an estimate, not a measurement.

quiz.statement: Every AI email uses a bottle of water.
quiz.why: Not proven. It's an estimate for one kind of email, based on guesses, not a measurement.

quiz.statement: A data center can strain a town's water on hot days even if its yearly use looks small.
quiz.why: The hottest days, when everyone needs water most, are when the strain shows.

quiz.statement: AI data centers are why my town has water restrictions.
quiz.why: Not proven. Drought maps and water company reports can't blame a shortage on one user.

water.carefulHeadline: AI data centers threaten water supplies in some dry US towns.
water.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “threaten” and talks only about some places, which matches what the evidence shows.
water.headlineSource: Said by: The Washington Post, in a September 2024 article about researchers' estimate of how much water AI chatbots use.
water.carefulSource: Our wording, based on a 2025 Bloomberg investigation into where AI data centers get their water.

jobs.headline: AI will take all our jobs.

keyWord.explanation: Even Musk said “probably”. The evidence shows AI changing tasks and slowing hiring for some young workers, not replacing every job.

jobs.scoreReason: The headline turns Musk's “probably” into a sure thing, and jumps from some tasks AI can do to every job.

claimDial.text: AI could eliminate half of US entry-level office jobs by about 2030.
claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: AI could wipe out half of US entry-level office jobs by about 2030.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

W1.reason: “Wipe out” adds drama to an expert's warning.

claimDial.text: AI will wipe out half of US entry-level office jobs by 2030.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P3.reason: Turns an expert's “could” into a sure thing.

W1.reason: “Wipe out” adds drama to an expert's warning.

claimDial.text: AI will take all our jobs.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: AI is already destroying jobs everywhere and will soon want every single one.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: Says jobs are already being destroyed everywhere, which the data don't show.

P2.reason: Stretches some tasks to every job.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W2.reason: Says AI “wants” jobs, when employers make those choices.

finePrint.label: What Musk actually said
finePrint.text: At a Paris tech conference in May 2024, Elon Musk said: “Probably none of us will have a job.” He added that work could become optional, like a hobby.

finePrint.label: “Exposed” isn't “at risk”
finePrint.text: It means AI could help with or do some tasks in a job. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics says it isn't a chance of losing your job.

finePrint.label: Fewer hires, not layoffs
finePrint.text: So far the change shows up mainly as weaker hiring of young people.

finePrint.label: The numbers so far
finePrint.text: In August 2026, employment of 22–25-year-olds was down 4.4% from a year earlier in the jobs where AI can do the most tasks, versus 2.0% in the jobs where it can do the fewest (figures from the payroll company ADP).

finePrint.label: The narrower warning
finePrint.text: Anthropic's CEO, whose company sells AI, warned in May 2025 that AI could eliminate half of entry-level office jobs within one to five years. That's a possible future, not a proven prediction.

quiz.why: Not proven. Even Musk said “probably”, and current data show no broad disruption.

quiz.statement: Young workers in AI-exposed jobs have seen weaker hiring.
quiz.why: Pay records from employers show it.

quiz.statement: AI caused that drop in hiring.
quiz.why: Not proven. Education, earlier trends and other factors haven't been ruled out.

jobs.carefulHeadline: AI could eliminate half of US entry-level office jobs by about 2030.
jobs.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “could”, and it's an expert's educated guess about the future, though nobody has been able to test the half-of-jobs number yet.
jobs.headlineSource: Said by: Elon Musk, at a tech conference in Paris in May 2024. CNN's headline was “Elon Musk says AI will take all our jobs.”
jobs.carefulSource: Our wording, based on a May 2025 warning by Dario Amodei, head of the AI company Anthropic.

energy-climate.headline: AI will only intensify climate change.

keyWord.explanation: “Only” rules out any climate benefit from AI. Those benefits are unproven, but so is the claim that there are none.

energy-climate.scoreReason: The headline says “will” and “only”, which leaves no room for the uncertainty or the possible benefits the evidence describes.

claimDial.text: AI's growing power use could raise US carbon emissions by 2030.
claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: AI's exploding power use could raise US carbon emissions by 2030.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

W1.reason: “Exploding” adds drama to a fast but measured rise.

claimDial.text: AI's exploding power use will raise US carbon emissions by 2030.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P3.reason: Turns “could” into a sure thing, though it depends on how power is made.

W1.reason: “Exploding” adds drama to a fast but measured rise.

claimDial.text: AI will only intensify climate change.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: AI is single-handedly destroying the planet and will make climate change unstoppable.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States as fact something no evidence shows.

P2.reason: Blames AI alone for a planet-wide problem.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W1.reason: “Destroying the planet” is alarm, not evidence.

W2.reason: Treats AI as the one acting, when people choose how to power it.

finePrint.label: Electricity isn't emissions
finePrint.text: The same power use can be clean or dirty depending on which plants make it.

finePrint.label: Not all data centers are AI
finePrint.text: All US data centers used 4.4% of US electricity in 2023; AI is one part of that.

finePrint.label: Green purchases have limits
finePrint.text: Buying renewable power over a year doesn't mean clean power every hour, in every place.

finePrint.label: Worldwide numbers
finePrint.text: The International Energy Agency says data centers worldwide used 485 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025 and expects about 950 by 2030, roughly double. That includes non-AI work.

finePrint.label: Could AI help the climate?
finePrint.text: Possibly, through things like smarter energy management, but those savings aren't proven to cancel out its emissions.

quiz.statement: If a company buys enough renewable power over a year, its AI runs on clean power every hour.
quiz.why: Yearly purchases don't match supply hour by hour.

quiz.statement: US emissions could fall overall while AI still adds emissions.
quiz.why: “Adds” means compared with a world without AI's extra power use.

quiz.statement: AI's climate benefits will cancel out its emissions.
quiz.why: Not proven. The savings depend on how widely AI is used for them, and using AI more can eat them up.

energy-climate.carefulHeadline: AI's growing power use could raise US carbon emissions by 2030.
energy-climate.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “could”, and there's a clear way it can happen: more demand for electricity, partly met by gas power plants.
energy-climate.headlineSource: Said by: historian Juan Cole, in the headline of a December 2025 article in The Nation.
energy-climate.carefulSource: Our wording, based on a 2025 Cornell University study of the AI data center boom's environmental impact.

creativity.headline: AI art is theft.

keyWord.explanation: Theft is a legal and moral judgment. US courts haven’t settled whether training AI on others’ work is legal, and one court found a specific use fair.

creativity.scoreReason: The headline treats a legal and moral judgment as settled fact, and applies it to all AI art.

claimDial.text: AI can spit out copies of copyrighted work it was trained on.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

claimDial.text: AI routinely churns out copies of the copyrighted work it learned from.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P2.reason: Says it happens routinely, when tests showed it with chosen works.

W1.reason: “Churns out” adds drama to what tests found.

claimDial.text: AI art is theft.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: AI is a plagiarism machine that steals every artist's work and will kill human creativity.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States wrongdoing as settled, when courts haven't decided.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W1.reason: “Plagiarism machine” is a label, not evidence.

W2.reason: Says AI “steals”, when companies choose what to train on.

finePrint.label: Learning vs. copying out
finePrint.text: Copying work to teach an AI is a separate legal question from the AI later spitting out a copy.

finePrint.label: Style isn't protected
finePrint.text: Imitating an artist's style usually isn't against copyright law; copying their actual work can be.

finePrint.label: Legal isn't the same as fair
finePrint.text: A court ruling can't settle whether creators should be asked or paid.

finePrint.label: Creators' income
finePrint.text: Image-making job posts on one global freelance site fell 17% after image generators appeared. That's one platform, not a US-wide figure.

quiz.statement: Copying an artist's style is copyright infringement.
quiz.why: Usually not. Style alone generally isn't protected.

quiz.statement: Researchers have pulled long book passages out of commercial AI models.
quiz.why: Shown in 2025 tests of four AI models that the public uses.

quiz.statement: Courts have ruled that AI art is theft.
quiz.why: US courts haven’t settled it, and one found a specific training use fair.

creativity.carefulHeadline: AI can reproduce copyrighted work from its training data.
creativity.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “can”, and experiments have shown that it happens.
creativity.headlineSource: Said by: researcher Trystan S. Goetze, as the title of a 2024 research paper.
creativity.carefulSource: Our wording, based on research showing AI models can repeat long passages from the work they were trained on.

privacy.headline: ChatGPT is sharing your secrets.

keyWord.explanation: “Sharing” suggests other people see your chats. What OpenAI describes is using chats to train its models, which you can turn off, plus limited access by staff for things like safety.

privacy.scoreReason: The headline calls training “sharing”, treats every chat as a secret, and ignores the settings that change what happens.

claimDial.text: ChatGPT may use your personal-account chats to train its AI, depending on your settings.
claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: ChatGPT may hoover up your personal chats to train its AI, depending on your settings.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

W1.reason: “Hoover up” adds drama to what the policy says.

claimDial.text: ChatGPT hoovers up your personal chats to train its AI.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P2.reason: Drops “depending on your settings”, so it sounds like every chat.

W1.reason: “Hoover up” adds drama to what the policy says.

claimDial.text: ChatGPT is sharing your secrets.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: ChatGPT is spying on everything you type and will sell your secrets to anyone who wants them.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States as fact something no evidence shows.

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W2.reason: Treats ChatGPT as a spy with its own plans.

finePrint.label: Three different things
finePrint.text: Training (improving the model), storing (keeping your chat) and access (who can see it) have separate settings and rules.

finePrint.label: Opting out isn't deleting
finePrint.text: Your chats stay saved until you delete them, and deletion has legal and security exceptions.

finePrint.label: Temporary Chat
finePrint.text: Not used for training, but kept for up to 30 days for safety checks. Saving it turns it into a normal chat.

finePrint.label: Shared links
finePrint.text: Anyone with a link to a chat you shared can see it.

finePrint.label: Depends on your state
finePrint.text: Californians have rights to see, correct and delete data; not every American does.

quiz.statement: Turning off training deletes my old chats.
quiz.why: Training and storage are separate. Delete chats separately.

quiz.statement: Thumbs-up or thumbs-down feedback may still be used even if I opt out.
quiz.why: OpenAI lists feedback as an exception.

quiz.statement: Other ChatGPT users can read my chats.
quiz.why: Not unless you share a link to a chat. Training and sharing are different things.

options.label: Personal account, training setting on
options.result: May be used to train OpenAI's models. Saved until you delete it.

options.label: Personal account, training setting off
options.result: Not used for training, except feedback you send with thumbs up or down. Still saved until you delete it.

options.label: Temporary Chat
options.result: Not used for training. Kept for up to 30 days for safety checks, then removed unless you save it.

options.label: Business or Enterprise account
options.result: Not used for training by default. Your organization controls who can see chats and how long they're kept.

privacy.carefulHeadline: ChatGPT may use your personal-account chats to train its AI, depending on your settings.
privacy.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version says “may” and “depending on your settings”, which matches what OpenAI's own policy says.
privacy.headlineSource: Said by: Tom's Guide, a tech advice website, in an April 2023 headline.
privacy.carefulSource: Our wording, based on OpenAI's own privacy settings, as explained by Tom's Guide.

existential-risk.headline: If anyone builds superintelligent AI, everyone dies.

keyWord.explanation: Stated as a certainty. The evidence shows real reasons for concern, not that extinction is guaranteed.

existential-risk.scoreReason: The headline says everyone will certainly die, and drops the authors' own condition about how this super-smart AI gets built.

claimDial.text: Future AI much smarter than people could pose serious risks, and experts disagree about how big they are.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

claimDial.text: Building superintelligent AI with 2025-era methods will kill everyone on Earth.
claimDial.origin: careful version

claimDial.text: Superintelligent AI built with today's methods will decide to kill us all.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P3.reason: Tells a guess about the future as a sure thing.

W2.reason: Says AI would “decide” to kill us; the authors' worry is about goals, not intent.

claimDial.text: If anyone builds superintelligent AI, everyone dies.
claimDial.origin: headline claim

claimDial.text: AI is already plotting to wipe us out, and it's only a matter of months.
claimDial.origin: Example wording we wrote and scored with the same checks

P1.reason: States as fact something no evidence shows.

P2.reason: Says today's AI, when the worry is about future AI.

P3.reason: Gives a sure timeline nobody can know.

W1.reason: “Plotting to wipe us out” is alarm, not evidence.

W2.reason: Says AI is plotting, as if it had human plans.

finePrint.label: Who says it
finePrint.text: Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, in their 2025 book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies.

finePrint.label: “Superintelligence”
finePrint.text: AI that is more capable than all of humanity combined, not today's chatbots.

finePrint.label: Not about hatred
finePrint.text: The authors' worry is AI pursuing goals and resources in ways that destroy what humans need to survive, not AI that hates us.

finePrint.label: Four different fears
finePrint.text: Everyone dying, a disaster that kills many people, people misusing AI, and losing control of AI are different things.

finePrint.label: What the tests showed
finePrint.text: AI models blackmailed people in made-up company scenarios (Anthropic, 2025). AI agents tried actions they weren't allowed to in UK government testing, and hacked a real website during standard skills tests (2026). The made-up scenarios hurt no one, and the UK attempts failed.

quiz.statement: AI systems have done things in tests their makers didn't intend.
quiz.why: Documented by Anthropic, the UK AI Security Institute and METR.

quiz.statement: Experts agree on how likely AI extinction is.
quiz.why: The 2026 International AI Safety Report records wide disagreement.

quiz.statement: AI risk is all made up.
quiz.why: The test incidents are real, even though they don't prove extinction.

existential-risk.carefulHeadline: Building superintelligent AI with 2025-era methods will kill everyone on Earth.
existential-risk.carefulScoreReason: The more careful version keeps the authors' condition, but “will” still sounds surer than the evidence allows.
existential-risk.headlineSource: Said by: AI-risk researchers Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares, as the title of their 2025 book.
existential-risk.carefulSource: Our wording of the full argument in Yudkowsky and Soares's book, which applies it to AI built with today's methods.
